topics_checked.note: EU free movement (FreizügG/EU §§2,4), non-EU study permit (§16b AufenthG), visa-free entry list (§41 AufenthV), blocked account amount (German mission Muscat page). Swiss rules not found on an official page today.
gesund.bund.de (Federal Ministry of Health portal), DAAD, TK (statutory insurer) on EU students who work.

§16b AufenthG (non-EU), TK Werkstudentenprivileg, Minijob-Zentrale student page, DRV press release on 2026 limits.

items.title: Right of residence for EU/EEA students (no visa)
items.title_it: Diritto di soggiorno per studenti UE/SEE (nessun visto)

applies_to.stay_duration: any; for stays beyond 3 months the non-economically-active conditions apply

items.summary: EU/EEA citizens need no visa or residence permit to study in Germany: they have freedom of movement. Students who are not working fall under the 'non-economically active' category, whose right of residence requires sufficient health insurance and sufficient means of subsistence (§4 FreizügG/EU). You still must register your address (Anmeldung).
items.notes: The statute text read today does not say how means and insurance are proven for students (e.g. whether a declaration is enough).

items.title: Residence for Swiss students
items.summary: Swiss citizens fall under the EU-Switzerland free movement agreement, not under §2 FreizügG/EU directly; the exact residence document requirements for Swiss students could not be confirmed on an official page today. Ask the local Ausländerbehörde.

items.title: Visa and residence permit for non-EU students (§16b AufenthG)
items.title_it: Visto e permesso di soggiorno per studenti extra-UE (§16b AufenthG)
items.summary: Non-EU students need a residence permit for study purposes (§16b AufenthG), normally entering with a national (D) visa from the German mission. The permit also covers preparatory measures such as a required language course or Studienkolleg. You must prove means equal to the BAföG need rate (§2(3) AufenthG): €992/month, i.e. €11,904/year, usually via a blocked account. Citizens of Australia, Israel, Japan, Canada, South Korea, New Zealand, UK and USA may enter visa-free and apply for the permit in Germany within 90 days (§41 AufenthV).
steps: Get admission (or conditional admission) from the university
Prove funds (blocked account €11,904/year or other accepted proof) and health insurance
Apply for the national visa at the German mission (unless your nationality is listed in §41 AufenthV)
After arrival: register your address, then apply for the residence permit at the Ausländerbehörde
items.cost: Blocked account: €11,904/year deposit, max €992/month withdrawal (current rate)
items.notes: €11,904/€992 read on the German embassy Muscat page today; the Auswärtiges Amt page says the amount follows the BAföG maximum rate, and 475+380+102+35 = €992 matches §§13, 13a BAföG. Citizens of Andorra, Brazil, El Salvador, Honduras, Monaco, San Marino may also apply after entry but only if they do not intend to work (§41(2) AufenthV). The BAföG reform bill (Drucksache 21/8405, not yet adopted on 2026-11-25) would raise the housing rate to €440 from summer semester 2027, which would raise this amount too.

items.title: Address registration (Anmeldung) within two weeks
items.title_it: Registrazione della residenza (Anmeldung) entro due settimane

applies_to.stay_duration: people with residence abroad: required if staying more than 3 months in the same dwelling

items.summary: Anyone who moves into a dwelling must register with the local registration office (Meldebehörde / Bürgeramt) within two weeks of moving in (§17 BMG). The landlord must give you a written move-in confirmation (Wohnungsgeberbestätigung, §19 BMG). If you normally live abroad and are not registered in Germany, the duty applies only once your stay exceeds three months (§27(2) BMG). Deregister within two weeks of moving out if you leave Germany.
steps: Get the Wohnungsgeberbestätigung from your landlord
Book an appointment at the Bürgeramt / Meldebehörde and register within 2 weeks
Keep the Meldebestätigung: it is needed for the bank, residence permit and tax ID

interpretations.hypothesis: An exchange student who keeps their home residence and stays in a German room for 3 months or less does not need to register (§27(2) BMG).
Any stay longer than 3 months (e.g. a full semester of about 5-6 months) triggers the 2-week registration duty, counted once the 3 months are exceeded.

items.title: Tax ID (Steuer-ID / IdNr) from the BZSt
items.summary: The 11-digit tax identification number is assigned automatically once the registration office has sent your data to the Federal Central Tax Office (BZSt), and it arrives only by letter (your name must be on the mailbox). If it has not arrived after three months, send the BZSt a copy of your ID and your Meldebestätigung. If you work in Germany without being registered there, the tax office of your employer's premises assigns it on request (form 010250).
steps: Give the number to your employer
items.notes: The BZSt gives no standard processing time. The KIT international office says it arrives 'a few weeks' after registration (https://www.intl.kit.edu/istudent/12592.php).

items.title: Mandatory health insurance at enrolment; statutory student rate until 30
items.title_it: Assicurazione sanitaria obbligatoria all'immatricolazione; tariffa studenti fino a 30 anni
items.summary: Everyone enrolling at a German university must prove health insurance; students are generally compulsorily insured in statutory insurance (GKV), which includes long-term care insurance. The student contribution is 70% of the general rate plus each fund's supplementary rate (DAAD: about €120-130/month). Compulsory student insurance generally ends in the semester you turn 30. You can apply for exemption with private insurance within the first 3 months, but the exemption is irrevocable for the whole degree.
items.deadline: Exemption request: within the first 3 months of studies
items.notes: Exceptions to the age-30 limit (illness over 3 months, caring for a child or relative) exist. The exact 2026 contribution depends on the chosen fund.

items.title: EU/EEA students: keeping home insurance with the EHIC
items.title_it: Studenti UE/SEE: mantenere l'assicurazione del proprio paese con la TEAM

other: only while not doing paid work in Germany

items.summary: Students from the EU, Norway, Iceland or Liechtenstein can keep their home statutory insurance if it is recognised: you usually need the European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) and a certificate from a German statutory insurer confirming exemption, which the university requires at enrolment. If you take a paid internship or a part-time job in Germany, German coverage is required.
items.authority: German statutory health insurer (issues the exemption certificate to the university)

interpretations.hypothesis: Exchange (Erasmus) students stay insured at home and the EHIC is sufficient; full-degree students can use the EHIC only if their residence and centre of life (Lebensmittelpunkt) stay in the home country, e.g. financed by parents. Students who receive German state study funding or plan to stay permanently leave home insurance and must join a German Krankenkasse. (Source is krankenkassen.de, a non-official comparison portal.)
DAAD states the EHIC route for EU/EEA students in general, without distinguishing exchange from full-degree students.

items.title: EU/EEA/Swiss students who work in Germany fall under German social insurance
items.title_it: Studenti UE/SEE/svizzeri che lavorano in Germania: si applica l'assicurazione tedesca

applies_to.min_work_hours: any paid job, including a Minijob, Werkstudent job or paid internship

items.summary: While only studying, EU/EEA/Swiss students follow the law of their country of residence. As soon as they take a Minijob, working-student job, paid voluntary internship or self-employment in Germany, German rules apply, so they normally need German student health insurance. Exception: students resident and insured in Denmark, Luxembourg or Austria keep their home cover for a Minijob. Mandatory internships required by the study rules do not change the situation.
items.notes: Source is Techniker Krankenkasse (a statutory insurer, public-law body). The TK page also mentions the UK and 'agreement countries' in the same rule.

items.title: Non-EU students: insurance proof for visa and enrolment
items.title_it: Studenti extra-UE: prova di assicurazione per visto e immatricolazione
items.summary: International students must show coverage equivalent to German standards at enrolment or, depending on the country, already for the visa. Under 30 the statutory student rate is available; from 30 the normal (much higher) statutory rate applies, and private student plans may be cheaper but vary in coverage. Choosing private insurance means you cannot switch back to statutory insurance later. DAAD scholarship holders are insured by the DAAD.

items.title: Right to a basic bank account (Basiskonto)
items.title_it: Diritto a un conto corrente di base (Basiskonto)
items.summary: Every consumer lawfully resident in the EU has a right to a basic payment account (Basiskonto), including people without a fixed address. Banks that offer consumer accounts must make an offer within ten business days of a complete request (§31 ZKG). Non-EU students usually also open a blocked account (Sperrkonto) before the visa.
items.deadline: Bank must answer within 10 business days
items.notes: Account fees for a Basiskonto are not researched. The Auswärtiges Amt page says its former list of blocked-account providers is under review.

items.title: Deutschlandsemesterticket (student Deutschlandticket)

other: enrolled at a university that has signed the Deutschlandsemesterticket agreement

items.summary: Since summer semester 2024 students can get the Deutschlandsemesterticket, valid like the Deutschlandticket on local and regional public transport across Germany, at 60% of the regular price. Whether your university offers it depends on negotiations with the student body and transport operators, so check with your university. It is usually paid with the semester contribution.
items.cost: 60% of the Deutschlandticket price (€63/month in 2026, €66.80/month from 1 Jan 2027)
items.authority: University / student union (AStA) with transport operators
items.notes: That it is paid via the semester contribution is common practice but was not stated on the page read today; check the university page.

items.title: Work limit for non-EU students: 140 working days per year
items.title_it: Limite di lavoro per studenti extra-UE: 140 giorni lavorativi all'anno
items.summary: A §16b study permit allows work totalling up to 140 working days per year. A day with up to 4 hours counts as a half day; alternatively, per calendar week, up to 20 hours during lecture periods count as 2.5 days, whichever is more favourable. Student assistant jobs at the university (studentische Nebentätigkeiten) do not count towards the limit.
items.notes: Read from the current statute text on 2026-11-25. Exchange students on a §16b permit are covered by the same paragraph. Work beyond these limits needs approval from the Ausländerbehörde.

items.title: Werkstudent rule: max 20 hours/week in term for social-insurance privileges
items.title_it: Regola Werkstudent: max 20 ore/settimana durante il semestre

applies_to.min_work_hours: more than a Minijob, up to 20 hours/week in lecture periods

items.summary: Regular students working up to 20 hours a week (all jobs added together, any pay level) pay only pension insurance, not health, care or unemployment insurance. More than 20 hours is allowed for up to 26 weeks (182 days) a year if it falls mainly on evenings, nights, weekends or semester breaks. Language-course and Studienkolleg participants, students on leave and students beyond 25 subject semesters are excluded. For non-EU students the 140-day limit applies on top.
items.notes: The TK page includes students of foreign universities among those the rule applies to.

items.title: Minijob: up to €603/month (2026)
items.summary: A Minijob with regular earnings of up to €603/month (2026) is free of health, care and unemployment insurance contributions for students; pension insurance applies but you can ask your employer to be exempted. Short-term jobs (max 3 months or 70 working days a year) have no earnings limit. The limit rises to €633/month on 1 Jan 2027.
items.notes: The €633 (2027) figure is from the Bundesregierung minimum-wage FAQ; the DRV press release does not mention 2027.

items.title: Statutory minimum wage €13.90/hour (2026), €14.60 from 2027

other: not for mandatory internships, internships up to 3 months, or minors without completed vocational training

items.summary: The statutory minimum wage is €13.90 gross per hour since 1 January 2026 and rises to €14.60 on 1 January 2027 (MiLoV5). It does not apply to mandatory internships required by study regulations, voluntary orientation or study-accompanying internships of up to 3 months, or minors without completed vocational training (§22 MiLoG). There is no separate youth rate for adults.
items.notes: Minors: §22(2) MiLoG refers to children and youths under the JArbSchG without completed vocational training.

items.title: Broadcasting fee (Rundfunkbeitrag) per dwelling
items.summary: Every dwelling pays €18.36/month (€55.08 per quarter), regardless of how many people live there or which devices they use. In a shared flat only one adult registers and pays and flatmates can split it. A dorm room opening onto a shared corridor counts as its own dwelling. For exemptions see the subsidies file.
